title: Branches are pointers
summary: A branch is a 41-byte file holding a commit hash. Creating, switching and deleting branches is cheap, so use them for everything.

steps.title: A branch is a sticky note
body: A branch is nothing more than a **name that points to a commit**. Creating one copies no files; it writes one hash into `.git/refs/heads/<name>`.
git switch -c feature          # new pointer at the current commit, HEAD -> feature
Commit twice on `feature`. Only the branch HEAD names moves:
`main` did not change. Two lines of work now exist side by side, and either can be merged, rebased or thrown away.

steps.prompt: Starting from `A---B (main, HEAD)`, you run these commands. Which commit does each branch point to? Answer `main -> ?` then `feature -> ?` on two lines.
code: git switch -c feature     # feature at B
steps.explain: Each commit moves only the branch HEAD names at that moment. C and D went on `feature`; after switching back, E went on `main` with B as its parent. The branches have **diverged** at B.

steps.prompt: Match the command to what it does to the pointers.
pairs: creates a pointer at HEAD but does not switch
creates a pointer and moves HEAD to it
deletes the pointer if its commits are merged
deletes the pointer even if commits would be unreachable

steps.prompt: You delete a branch with `git branch -D experiment`. What happens to its commits?
options: They still exist in the object database; no name points to them, and the reflog can find them until garbage collection
They are pushed to the remote first
steps.explain: Deleting a branch only removes the name. Unreachable commits are cleaned up by `git gc` much later (after the reflog expires).

steps.prompt: Complete the commands: list all branches including remote-tracking ones, then show which branches are already merged into `main`.
steps.explain: `--merged` is how you find branches that are safe to delete. `--no-merged` shows the ones still holding unmerged work.

steps.title: Ancestors
body: Commit X is an **ancestor** of Y if you can reach X by following parent pointers from Y.
- B is an ancestor of both C and E.
- C is **not** an ancestor of E, nor E of C: the branches diverged.

This one question drives a lot of Git: *Is the tip of main an ancestor of feature?* If yes, `main` can simply slide forward to feature (a **fast-forward**, next lesson). *Is my branch's tip an ancestor of the remote's?* If not, `git push` is rejected (module 4).

steps.prompt: In the diagram above, is the first commit an ancestor of the second?
steps.explain: Follow parent arrows only backwards in time: from E you reach D, B, A. Never C.

steps.title: Is it an ancestor?
prompt: Model the commit graph as `parents`: each commit id maps to an array of parent ids (empty for the first commit, two for a merge).

Write `IsAncestor(string a, string b, parents)` returning true if `a` is `b` or can be reached from `b` by following parents. Use a stack or queue and a visited set (merges mean you can reach a commit twice).
starter: static bool IsAncestor(string a, string b, Dictionary<string, string[]> parents)
solution: static bool IsAncestor(string a, string b, Dictionary<string, string[]> parents)
hints: Pop a commit: if it is `a`, return true; otherwise push its parents.
A `HashSet<string>` stops you walking the same history twice.
template: Dojo.Eq("B is an ancestor of E", true, IsAncestor("B", "E", dojoG));
Dojo.Eq("C is not an ancestor of E", false, IsAncestor("C", "E", dojoG));
Dojo.Eq("a commit is its own ancestor", true, IsAncestor("E", "E", dojoG));
Dojo.Eq("both sides of a merge are ancestors", true, IsAncestor("C", "M", dojoG) && IsAncestor("D", "M", dojoG));
Dojo.Eq("children are not ancestors", false, IsAncestor("M", "A", dojoG));
